EMINENT DOMAIN AND INVERSE CONDEMNATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield · Pat Morgan

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — INFORMATIONAL ONLY
This information sheet describes, in general terms, California's constitutional and statutory framework governing eminent domain and inverse condemnation. It is prepared in connection with the real property located at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield, of record in the name of Pat Morgan, and the public project or action described as: Widening of Main Street between 3rd and 5th Avenue, involving City of Springfield. This sheet is informational only. It does not itself commence, oppose, settle, or resolve any eminent domain proceeding or inverse condemnation claim; it does not determine whether any specific act, plan, project, or occurrence involving City of Springfield constitutes a "taking" or a "damaging" of the property described above, whether any resolution of necessity has been validly adopted, or whether any particular compensation figure is accurate or adequate. It states only what the California Constitution and California's Eminent Domain Law generally provide.

STATE CONSTITUTIONAL FOUNDATION — TAKING OR DAMAGING FOR PUBLIC USE
Article I, section 19, subdivision (a) of the California Constitution provides that private property may be taken or damaged for a public use, and only when just compensation — ascertained by a jury unless waived — has first been paid to, or into court for, the owner. This text protects against both a "taking" of private property and a "damaging" of it, and by its own terms it reaches property that is merely damaged for a public use, not only property that is physically taken. This is broader than the wording of the Takings Clause of the Fifth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which by its text addresses property that is "taken," without a corresponding reference to property that is "damaged." Article I, section 19(a) also authorizes the Legislature to allow a condemning entity to take possession of the property after commencing an eminent domain proceeding, upon depositing in court, and promptly releasing to the owner, the amount the court determines to be the probable just compensation. Separate subdivisions of the same section — (b) through (e) — restrict the use of eminent domain to acquire an owner-occupied residence for the purpose of conveying it to a private person, subject to listed exceptions for protecting public health and safety, preventing serious repeated criminal activity, responding to an emergency, remedying environmental contamination, and acquiring property for a public work or improvement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Private property may be taken or damaged for a public use and only when just compensation, ascertained by a jury unless waived, has first been paid to, or into court for, the owner."
  — California Constitution, Cal. Const., art. I, § 19, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=SEC.%2019.&lawCode=CONS&article=I)
  Known gap: This clause quotes and describes subdivision (a) of Article I, section 19, which is the operative taking/damaging and just-compensation text. It also summarizes, without separately quoting, subdivisions (b) through (e) of the same section (the owner-occupied-residence restriction and its exceptions and definitions) — those subdivisions are part of the same constitutional section already cited, not an independent source. The comparison to the U.S. Constitution's Fifth Amendment states the well-established textual difference between the two provisions' wording but is not itself supported by a citation to federal constitutional text fetched in this research.

THE EMINENT DOMAIN LAW — PUBLIC USE AND NECESSITY FINDINGS
California Code of Civil Procedure sections 1230.010 through 1273.050 are known and may be cited as the "Eminent Domain Law," and, except as otherwise specifically provided by another statute, this is the framework under which the power of eminent domain may be exercised in California. Under this law, the power of eminent domain may be exercised to acquire property only for a public use; where the Legislature has provided by statute that a given use, purpose, object, or function is one for which eminent domain may be exercised, that statutory designation is itself treated as a declaration that the use is a public use. Before property may be acquired for a proposed project, the statute requires that all of the following be established: that the public interest and necessity require the project; that the project is planned or located in the manner that will be most compatible with the greatest public good and the least private injury; and that the property sought to be acquired is necessary for the project.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "This title shall be known and may be cited as the Eminent Domain Law."
  — California Code of Civil Procedure, Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1230.010 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1230.010.&lawCode=CCP)
  "Except as otherwise specifically provided by statute, the power of eminent domain may be exercised only as provided in this title."
  — California Code of Civil Procedure, Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1230.020 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1230.020.&lawCode=CCP)
  "The power of eminent domain may be exercised to acquire property only for a public use."
  — California Code of Civil Procedure, Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1240.010 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1240.010.&lawCode=CCP)
  "The power of eminent domain may be exercised to acquire property for a proposed project only if all of the following are established:"
  — California Code of Civil Procedure, Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1240.030 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1240.030.&lawCode=CCP)
  Known gap: The four citations below are separate sections within the same statutory title — Code of Civil Procedure, Title 7, the Eminent Domain Law (§§ 1230.010–1273.050) — rather than independently enacted, unrelated statutes; they should be read together as one integrated legislative scheme, not as separately corroborating sources. This clause states only the general public-use and necessity-findings requirement. It does not describe the procedural steps of an eminent domain action itself (service of the complaint, deposit and possession, trial on compensation, entry of judgment, and so on), which are addressed by other sections of the same title not covered here.

RESOLUTION OF NECESSITY — PREREQUISITE TO FILING
Before a public entity may exercise the power of eminent domain, the Eminent Domain Law requires that its governing body first adopt a resolution of necessity meeting statutory requirements; a public entity may not commence an eminent domain proceeding until it has done so. Among other things, the resolution must contain a general statement of the public use for which the property is to be taken and a reference to the statute authorizing the acquisition; a description of the property's general location and extent, with sufficient detail for reasonable identification; and the governing body's declaration that it has found and determined that the public interest and necessity require the project, that the project is planned or located in the manner most compatible with the greatest public good and least private injury, and that the property is necessary for the project. Unless a greater vote is required by statute, charter, or ordinance, the resolution must be adopted by a vote of two-thirds of all members of the entity's governing body. Except as otherwise provided by statute, a resolution of necessity adopted in this manner conclusively establishes the matters it addresses (the public-interest, compatible-location, and necessity findings).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A public entity may exercise the power of eminent domain only if it has adopted a resolution of necessity that meets the requirements of Article 2 (commencing with Section 1245.210) of Chapter 4."
  — California Code of Civil Procedure, Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1240.040 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1240.040.&lawCode=CCP)
  "A public entity may not commence an eminent domain proceeding until its governing body has adopted a resolution of necessity that meets the requirements of this article."
  — California Code of Civil Procedure, Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1245.220 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1245.220.&lawCode=CCP)
  "In addition to other requirements imposed by law, the resolution of necessity shall contain all of the following:"
  — California Code of Civil Procedure, Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1245.230 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1245.230.&lawCode=CCP)
  "Unless a greater vote is required by statute, charter, or ordinance, the resolution shall be adopted by a vote of two-thirds of all the members of the governing body of the public entity."
  — California Code of Civil Procedure, Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1245.240 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1245.240.&lawCode=CCP)
  "Except as otherwise provided by statute, a resolution of necessity adopted by the governing body of the public entity pursuant to this article conclusively establishes the matters referred to in Section 1240.030."
  — California Code of Civil Procedure, Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1245.250 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1245.250.&lawCode=CCP)
  Known gap: The citations below are all provisions of the same statutory article — Code of Civil Procedure, Chapter 4, Article 2 (Resolution of Necessity, §§ 1245.210–1245.270) — plus one cross-referenced section from the same title's general provisions (§ 1240.040); they are not independent sources of one another and should be read as one integrated procedural scheme. This clause omits the statute's carve-outs from the conclusive-presumption rule (§ 1245.250, subds. (b)–(d)), under which a resolution creates only a rebuttable presumption, rather than a conclusive one, for certain takings of local public-utility property or property not located entirely within the acquiring entity's boundaries — those exceptions were reviewed in the same fetch but are not restated here in full. It also does not describe the separate statutory requirement that the public entity make a precondemnation offer to the property owner before adopting the resolution (Gov. Code § 7267.2, referenced but not independently verified here) or the emergency-project exception to that offer requirement.

JUST COMPENSATION STANDARD — FAIR MARKET VALUE
The Eminent Domain Law's own compensation provisions describe how "just compensation" for property taken is measured. Compensation is awarded for the property taken, and the measure of that compensation is the property's fair market value. The statute defines fair market value as the highest price, on the date of valuation, that would be agreed to by a seller who is willing to sell but under no particular or urgent necessity to do so and not obliged to sell, and a buyer who is ready, willing, and able to buy but under no particular necessity to do so, with each party dealing with the other with full knowledge of all the uses and purposes for which the property is reasonably adaptable and available. Where there is no relevant, comparable market for the property taken, the statute instead defines fair market value as the property's value on the date of valuation as determined by any method of valuation that is just and equitable.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Compensation shall be awarded for the property taken. The measure of this compensation is the fair market value of the property taken."
  — California Code of Civil Procedure, Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1263.310 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1263.310.&lawCode=CCP)
  "The fair market value of the property taken is the highest price on the date of valuation that would be agreed to by a seller, being willing to sell but under no particular or urgent necessity for so doing, nor obliged to sell, and a buyer, being ready, willing, and able to buy but under no particular necessity for so doing, each dealing with the other with full knowledge of all the uses and purposes for which the property is reasonably adaptable and available."
  — California Code of Civil Procedure, Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1263.320 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1263.320.&lawCode=CCP)
  Known gap: The two citations below are adjacent sections of the same statutory article — Code of Civil Procedure, Chapter 9, Article 4 (Measure of Compensation for Property Taken, §§ 1263.310–1263.330) — and are not independent of one another. This clause addresses only the measure of compensation for property actually taken. It does not describe the statute's separate rules for severance damage to a remainder parcel, for benefits offset against severance damage, or for loss of business goodwill, all of which are addressed elsewhere in the same chapter and are not covered here.

INVERSE CONDEMNATION — A PROPERTY OWNER'S REVERSE ACTION
California recognizes a cause of action called "inverse condemnation," by which a property owner — rather than the public entity — brings an action against a public entity for having taken or damaged private property for a public use without the entity having exercised the formal eminent domain procedure. Unlike eminent domain, in which the public entity commences the proceeding, an inverse condemnation action is initiated by the affected property owner. California's statutes governing litigation costs refer to and presuppose the existence of an "inverse condemnation proceeding" as an established type of action, but they do not themselves define when a taking or damaging has occurred; based on the sources reviewed for this document, the cause of action itself derives directly from the state constitutional "taken or damaged" language, as interpreted by California courts, rather than from a separate statute defining its elements. In Albers v. County of Los Angeles (1965) 62 Cal.2d 250 — a case arising from a major landslide that destroyed and damaged homes near a county road project — the California Supreme Court held that liability for inverse condemnation under this constitutional provision does not depend on a showing that the public entity acted negligently: the court concluded that, with certain stated exceptions, any actual physical injury to real property proximately caused by a public improvement as deliberately designed and constructed is compensable under the constitutional provision, whether or not the injury was foreseeable.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Private property may be taken or damaged for a public use and only when just compensation, ascertained by a jury unless waived, has first been paid to, or into court for, the owner."
  — California Constitution, Cal. Const., art. I, § 19, subd. (a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=SEC.%2019.&lawCode=CONS&article=I)
  "In any inverse condemnation proceeding, the court rendering judgment for the plaintiff by awarding compensation, or the attorney representing the public entity who effects a settlement of that proceeding, shall determine and award or allow to the plaintiff, as a part of that judgment or settlement, a sum that will, in the opinion of the court, reimburse the plaintiff’s reasonable costs, disbursements, and expenses"
  — California Code of Civil Procedure, Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1036 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1036.&lawCode=CCP)
  "For these reasons we conclude that in the appeal of the county the judgments should be affirmed on the ground that with the exceptions stated in Gray, supra, and Archer, supra, any actual physical injury to real property proximately caused by the improvement as deliberately designed and"
  — Albers v. County of Los Angeles, 62 Cal. 2d 250 (1965) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/5607385/albers-v-county-of-los-angeles/)
  Known gap: The constitutional citation in this clause is the same provision — Cal. Const., art. I, § 19, subd. (a) — already quoted in this document's constitutional-foundation clause; it is not an independent source of that clause's citation, though it is being applied here to a different point (the inverse-condemnation cause of action rather than the general taking/damaging and just-compensation rule). The Code of Civil Procedure section and the Albers opinion are independent, differently-typed sources (a statute and a judicial opinion) that corroborate the existence and general contours of the doctrine. This clause describes one landmark, and long-standing, California Supreme Court case on the no-fault character of inverse condemnation liability; it does not catalog the large body of subsequent case law refining causation, design-immunity, and comparative-fault questions in inverse condemnation, none of which is addressed here. It also does not identify any statute that comprehensively defines the elements of an inverse condemnation cause of action, because none was found in this research — if such a statute exists for a particular context (for example, certain flood-control or public-utility contexts), it was not verified here and is not described.

LITIGATION EXPENSES IN EMINENT DOMAIN AND INVERSE CONDEMNATION PROCEEDINGS
California statutes address a property owner's recovery of litigation expenses differently in eminent domain proceedings and in inverse condemnation proceedings. In an eminent domain proceeding, the plaintiff public entity must file and serve its final offer of compensation, and the defendant property owner must file and serve a final demand, at least 20 days before trial on compensation issues; if, on the defendant's motion made within 30 days after entry of judgment, the court finds that the public entity's offer was unreasonable and the property owner's demand was reasonable in light of the evidence and the compensation awarded, the property owner's recoverable costs must include the owner's "litigation expenses" — defined by the statute as the party's reasonable attorney's fees and costs, including reasonable expert witness and appraiser fees. In an inverse condemnation proceeding, a different statute requires the court rendering judgment for the plaintiff, or the public entity's attorney in effecting a settlement, to award the plaintiff a sum reimbursing the plaintiff's reasonable costs, disbursements, and expenses — including reasonable attorney, appraisal, and engineering fees — actually incurred because of the proceeding, whether in the trial court or on any appeal on which the plaintiff prevails on any issue.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If the court, on motion of the defendant made within 30 days after entry of judgment, finds that the offer of the plaintiff was unreasonable and that the demand of the defendant was reasonable viewed in the light of the evidence admitted and the compensation awarded in the proceeding, the costs allowed pursuant to Section 1268.710 shall include the defendant’s litigation expenses."
  — California Code of Civil Procedure, Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1250.410 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1250.410.&lawCode=CCP)
  "In any inverse condemnation proceeding, the court rendering judgment for the plaintiff by awarding compensation, or the attorney representing the public entity who effects a settlement of that proceeding, shall determine and award or allow to the plaintiff, as a part of that judgment or settlement, a sum that will, in the opinion of the court, reimburse the plaintiff’s reasonable costs, disbursements, and expenses, including reasonable attorney, appraisal, and engineering fees, actually incurred because of that proceeding in the trial court or in any appellate proceeding in which the plaintiff prevails on any issue in that proceeding."
  — California Code of Civil Procedure, Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1036 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1036.&lawCode=CCP)
  Known gap: The two statutes cited are independent of one another — they are codified in different titles of the Code of Civil Procedure (one within the Eminent Domain Law itself; the other within the general costs provisions applicable to civil actions) and govern different proceeding types. The eminent domain fee-shifting rule is conditional and requires a specific comparison of the entity's offer, the owner's demand, and the compensation ultimately awarded; the inverse condemnation costs statute does not use that same offer/demand comparison and instead turns on the plaintiff obtaining a judgment or settlement in its favor. This clause states the general operation of each provision; it does not describe every procedural detail (for example, the role of a deposit under a separate chapter, or the treatment of offers made under the precondemnation-offer statute) that a court may consider in applying either rule.

In an eminent domain proceeding, the plaintiff public entity must file and serve its final offer of compensation, and the defendant property owner must file and serve a final demand, at least 20 days before trial on compensation issues; if, on the defendant's motion made within 30 days after entry of judgment, the court finds that the public entity's offer was unreasonable and the property owner's demand was reasonable in light of the evidence and the compensation awarded, the property owner's recoverable costs must include the owner's "litigation expenses" — defined by the statute as the party's reasonable attorney's fees and costs, including reasonable expert witness and appraiser fees. In an inverse condemnation proceeding, a different statute requires the court rendering judgment for the plaintiff, or the public entity's attorney in effecting a settlement, to award the plaintiff a sum reimbursing the plaintiff's reasonable costs, disbursements, and expenses — including reasonable attorney, appraisal, and engineering fees — actually incurred because of the proceeding, whether in the trial court or on any appeal on which the plaintiff prevails on any issue.

citations.quote: If the court, on motion of the defendant made within 30 days after entry of judgment, finds that the offer of the plaintiff was unreasonable and that the demand of the defendant was reasonable viewed in the light of the evidence admitted and the compensation awarded in the proceeding, the costs allowed pursuant to Section 1268.710 shall include the defendant’s litigation expenses.

In any inverse condemnation proceeding, the court rendering judgment for the plaintiff by awarding compensation, or the attorney representing the public entity who effects a settlement of that proceeding, shall determine and award or allow to the plaintiff, as a part of that judgment or settlement, a sum that will, in the opinion of the court, reimburse the plaintiff’s reasonable costs, disbursements, and expenses, including reasonable attorney, appraisal, and engineering fees, actually incurred because of that proceeding in the trial court or in any appellate proceeding in which the plaintiff prevails on any issue in that proceeding.

expectedJSON.gap: The two statutes cited are independent of one another — they are codified in different titles of the Code of Civil Procedure (one within the Eminent Domain Law itself; the other within the general costs provisions applicable to civil actions) and govern different proceeding types. The eminent domain fee-shifting rule is conditional and requires a specific comparison of the entity's offer, the owner's demand, and the compensation ultimately awarded; the inverse condemnation costs statute does not use that same offer/demand comparison and instead turns on the plaintiff obtaining a judgment or settlement in its favor. This clause states the general operation of each provision; it does not describe every procedural detail (for example, the role of a deposit under a separate chapter, or the treatment of offers made under the precondemnation-offer statute) that a court may consider in applying either rule.
